title: A Low-Cost and Transferable Remote Sensing Framework for Monitoring Urban Runoff and Operational Assessment of Flood Susceptibility in Rapidly Urbanizing Tropical Cities: The Case of Abidjan, Côte d'Ivoire
content: Tropical cities are experiencing rapid urbanization, often without adequate resources to monitor its effects on runoff processes or to support flood forecasting and early warning. This study proposes a low-cost and potentially transferable remote sensing framework to assess the evolution of urban runoff susceptibility in rapidly urbanizing tropical watersheds. The framework combines multi-temporal satellite imagery, urban-adapted spectral indices, supervised Random Forest land use/land cover (LULC) classification, and hydrological analysis based on the Soil Conservation Service Curve Number (SCS-CN) method. It was applied to the Gourou (28 km²) and Bonoumin (46 km²) watersheds in Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire, for 2002, 2016, and 2024. Spatially distributed runoff was estimated using rainfall scenarios of 30, 70, 100, and 302 mm and subsequently translated into runoff susceptibility indicators. The results reveal substantial urban expansion, particularly in Bonoumin, accompanied by increasing CN values and declining infiltration potential. Under the 30 mm rainfall scenario, the runoff coefficient increased from 0.29 to 0.53 in Bonoumin between 2002 and 2024, reflecting a marked hydrological transformation, while Gourou maintained a comparatively high runoff response throughout the study period. Under the extreme 302 mm scenario, runoff coefficients reached 0.94 in both watersheds in 2024. High and Very High runoff susceptibility classes also expanded substantially under extreme rainfall conditions. Although direct validation against observed discharge was not possible because both watersheds are ungauged, the identified trends are consistent with land-cover changes, previous studies, and the established SCS-CN hydrologic soil-group framework. The proposed framework therefore provides spatially explicit indicators that can support urban planning, flood preparedness, risk management, and early warning in data-scarce tropical cities.
